title: Canada's Pacific Link pipeline fight
dek: Ottawa's first use of its fast-track major-projects law, for an oil pipeline from Alberta to the B.C. coast, the First Nations court challenge and consultation dispute that followed, and the new bill that would widen the law.
summary: In June 2025 Parliament passed Bill C-5, whose Building Canada Act lets the federal cabinet designate projects as being in the national interest and fast-track their approval. In November 2025 Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith signed an agreement backing a new oil pipeline to the B.C. coast. Alberta applied in July 2026 for a route from Bruderheim, near Edmonton, to the southwest B.C. coast near Delta, largely following the Trans Mountain corridor, and Ottawa agreed with B.C. to keep the north coast oil tanker ban.

On October 1, 2026, Ottawa designated the pipeline, now called Pacific Link, as the first project of national interest. The government says it would carry an extra one million barrels of crude a day, be owned equally by Canada and Alberta with Pembina Pipeline as a private partner, and offer Indigenous communities at least a 10% stake. The Major Projects Office aims to have the conditions for construction in place by September 2027. On October 7 Cold Lake First Nations asked the Federal Court to quash the designation, saying it was not consulted; on November 2 nine B.C. First Nations announced they had filed their own applications.

The Union of BC Indian Chiefs, the BC Assembly of First Nations and several nations along the route say consultation was rushed and that the designation overrides their rights; at least one oilsands-region chief says he welcomes the equity stake. The federal government says it consulted more than 130 communities and that the duty to consult is unchanged. A second bill, C-39, which would extend fast-track powers, passed second reading on October 8 and is before a House committee. The B.C. Conservatives won the October 24 provincial election, and First Nations leaders met the prime minister and most premiers in Ottawa on October 26. Washington state officials and tribes have separately raised concerns about the pipeline's planned tanker traffic through the Salish Sea.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Bill C-5 receives royal assent after the Senate passes it unamended. Its Building Canada Act lets cabinet fast-track projects it designates as in the national interest; some senators opposed it over Indigenous rights.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Nine Ontario First Nations ask the Ontario Superior Court to declare Bill C-5 and Ontario's Bill 5 unconstitutional and seek an injunction against parts of both laws.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Carney and Smith sign a memorandum of understanding in Calgary backing a pipeline of at least one million barrels a day to B.C.'s northwest coast, with Indigenous co-ownership. Ottawa commits to adjusting the north coast tanker ban if needed.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: B.C. Premier David Eby says the project has "no proponent, no route, no money, no First Nations support". Coastal First Nations say the tanker ban is not negotiable, and the Union of BC Indian Chiefs rejects the agreement.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Alberta submits its pipeline application to the federal Major Projects Office, proposing a route from Bruderheim to B.C.'s southwest coast that largely follows the Trans Mountain corridor, with Trans Mountain Corporation and Pembina Pipeline as partners. Alberta estimates the cost at $35.2 billion to $43.7 billion.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Ottawa and B.C. sign an agreement that keeps the north coast tanker ban and includes federal infrastructure funding. B.C. says it is not required to support any pipeline, and Eby says the province will not go to court against it.

events.label: reported
events.text: Tsawwassen First Nation, near the proposed terminal, says it has not been consulted and has not taken a position on the southern route.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: The Major Projects Office's engagement with Indigenous peoples on the proposed designation closes, after the deadline was extended from August 28. A federal summary says groups reported lacking information on routing, marine shipping and impacts on their rights.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: The government tables Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act, which would set one-year federal review timelines and let cabinet designate "regions of national interest" with fast-track treatment.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: In Fort McMurray, Carney and Smith announce that the pipeline, renamed Pacific Link, is the first project designated in the national interest under the Building Canada Act. The government says it would carry an extra one million barrels a day, mainly to Asian markets.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: The government says Canada and Alberta will own the project equally, with Trans Mountain Corporation leading and Pembina Pipeline as a private investor, and that Indigenous communities will be offered at least 10% through loan guarantees. The Major Projects Office aims to finalise conditions by September 1, 2027.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: The Union of BC Indian Chiefs rejects the designation, saying consultation was incomplete. Semá:th First Nation, Coldwater Indian Band, Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation and Heiltsuk Nation leaders also criticise the project or the process; Coldwater says it is considering legal action.

events.label: reported
events.text: Fort McKay First Nation's chief says he is excited about becoming an equity stakeholder, while raising environmental concerns. The Assembly of First Nations says it sees "many red flags" in the designation, The Canadian Press reports.

events.label: reported
events.text: A lawyer for several affected First Nations tells CTV News many of them are not opposed to a pipeline but are concerned about consultation, and that a 10% stake is too low. Business groups welcome the designation; NDP Leader Avi Lewis and Environmental Defence oppose it.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Cold Lake First Nations, in Alberta's oilsands region, files for judicial review in the Federal Court, saying the Major Projects Office did not consult it. It asks the court to quash the designation.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Bill C-39 passes second reading in the House of Commons, 296 to 26, with Liberal and Conservative support, and goes to a special committee.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: The Chiefs of Ontario, the BC Assembly of First Nations, the AFN Quebec-Labrador and Nishnawbe Aski Nation reject Bill C-39 in a joint statement, saying it would override treaty and constitutional rights.

events.label: reported
events.text: Leaders of six Métis nations around Fort McMurray say they were not consulted before Ottawa designated the pipeline and call Carney's reconciliation commitment "a hollow promise", Yahoo News Canada reports. They say they do not oppose the pipeline itself but fear the oilsands expansion it would require; Willow Lake Métis Nation president Stella Lavallee says of the offered 10% Indigenous equity stake, "Zero per cent of 10 per cent is zero per cent."

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Major Projects Office CEO Dawn Farrell faces chiefs at the BC Assembly of First Nations meeting in Vancouver. Chiefs say they had 11 working days to review the designation; Farrell says the office wants to do better.

events.label: reported
events.text: The BC Assembly of First Nations meeting passes a resolution calling on Carney to halt the Building Canada Act and to repeal Bill C-39 if it passes, The Canadian Press reports.

events.label: reported
events.text: AFN B.C. Regional Chief Terry Teegee calls Pacific Link "a pipeline to more litigation" and says it has divided First Nations that would benefit from those that would not, APTN reports.

events.label: reported
events.text: Ministers Dominic LeBlanc and Steven MacKinnon defend Bill C-39 at a House of Commons committee; LeBlanc says it does not lessen the duty to consult. The Narwhal reports the government aims to pass the bill by the end of 2026.

events.label: reported
events.text: Washington state officials and tribes step up opposition to Pacific Link's planned tanker traffic through the Salish Sea: Gov. Bob Ferguson and state ecology director Casey Sixkiller say they are "disappointed" by the fast-tracking and want Canada to commit to stronger spill-response capacity; the Swinomish Indian Tribal Community's chairman calls the added shipping an "existential threat" to treaty fishing rights and salmon; the Affiliated Tribes of Northwest Indians pass a resolution against the project; and San Juan County officials and Rep. Rick Larsen (D-Wash.) raise vessel-traffic and spill-response concerns, Cascadia Daily and the Washington State Standard report.

events.label: reported
events.text: Cold Lake First Nations Chief Kelsey Jacko says "a lot of conflict" has surrounded which Alberta chiefs will attend Monday's First Nations-First Ministers meeting, since Alberta has no AFN regional chief; three Cree Nations, Onion Lake, Tsuut'ina and Saddle Lake, issue cease-and-desist notices telling the Assembly of First Nations not to speak for them, APTN reports. Jacko says he is attending because "nobody is going to be speaking for me, for our rights or for our people," and that his nation remains in court with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

events.label: reported
events.text: AFN National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak says the agenda for Monday's meeting with Carney and the premiers is still being negotiated and calls the relationship with Ottawa "very fragile"; only the opening prayer and remarks will be livestreamed, APTN reports. Onion Lake Cree Nation plans a National Day of Action outside the Ottawa venue on Monday, and AFN has circulated a draft proposal for a First Nations-controlled sovereign wealth fund that Woodhouse Nepinak says carries "no commitment yet."

events.label: confirmed
events.text: British Columbia's Conservative Party wins a majority government in the snap election Premier David Eby called for October 24, in which the pipeline was a campaign issue, CTV News declares; CBC News and The Canadian Press separately report the Conservative majority win. Eby resigns as leader of the B.C. NDP, saying in his concession speech, "I accept full responsibility." Final seat totals were not yet available.

events.label: reported
events.text: The Canadian Press reports Monday's meeting would be the first gathering of its kind since the 2005 Kelowna meeting between First Nations and Ottawa. Jeff Copenace, of Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation, says he worries a focus on economic development will crowd out action on addictions, homelessness and suicide; longtime AFN critic Russ Diabo says he distrusts the Assembly and is organising a separate meeting and protest, saying he fears the outcome is predetermined.

events.label: reported
events.text: Carney, most premiers and Assembly of First Nations leaders held their first such meeting since 2005; Carney said ministers will work with First Nations on moving beyond the Indian Act. National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said it "can't just be about ramming through major projects as fast as we can," while young protesters outside said major projects need their "free, prior and informed consent," The Canadian Press reports.

events.label: reported
events.text: Imperial Oil's chief executive said he is encouraged by progress toward a binding Pathways carbon-storage agreement with Ottawa and Alberta, a condition for the Pacific Link pipeline, though "there's still a lot of work left to do," BNN Bloomberg reports. A non-binding July memorandum set a Nov. 15 target for binding agreements; he described recent production problems as one-offs.

events.label: reported
events.text: Tsartlip First Nation, on Vancouver Island, files for judicial review in the Federal Court of the Pacific Link national-interest designation, saying federal consultation was rushed and ignored its treaty rights, CTV News reports. The report says Ottawa did not respond before publication; the designation came on October 1, less than two weeks after the nation set out its concerns.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Nine B.C. First Nations announce Federal Court applications to quash the Pacific Link national-interest designation, saying Ottawa did not adequately consult them. Ottawa says it consulted more than 110 Indigenous communities and will offer a minimum 10 per cent ownership stake, The Globe and Mail and the Vancouver Sun report; Cold Lake First Nation filed the first challenge in October.

events.label: pending
events.text: Whether binding Pathways carbon-storage agreements are signed by the November 15 target, the federal response to the First Nations court challenges, and the stance of the incoming B.C. Conservative government on Pacific Link. Still being checked.

claims.title: Was consultation on the designation adequate?
claims.label: disputed
claims.a: The government says the Major Projects Office consulted more than 130 Indigenous communities over three months and held more than 140 meetings; the Privy Council Office says senior officials meet communities when asked.
claims.b: Cold Lake First Nations says it was not consulted at all; B.C. chiefs say they had 11 working days; the Union of BC Indian Chiefs calls the process incomplete; Tsawwassen First Nation said in July it had not been consulted.
claims.status: The Federal Court has not ruled on Cold Lake First Nations' application.

claims.title: Does the fast-track law weaken Indigenous rights?
claims.label: disputed
claims.a: Ministers say the duty to consult is unchanged and that "a more efficient process does not mean a less rigorous one"; Carney has said the agenda will not interfere with Canada's obligations under the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
claims.b: First Nations organisations say the Building Canada Act and Bill C-39 override treaty and constitutional rights and that one year is not enough for free, prior and informed consent.
claims.status: Bill C-39 is in committee. We have not found a ruling in the 2025 Ontario challenge to Bill C-5.

claims.title: Do First Nations support the pipeline?
claims.label: disputed
claims.a: Fort McKay First Nation's chief says he welcomes an equity stake; a lawyer for several affected nations says many are not opposed to a pipeline but want proper consultation. The government offers at least a 10% Indigenous stake.
claims.b: The Union of BC Indian Chiefs, Coastal First Nations and several nations along the route oppose the project or the designation; the AFN B.C. regional chief says it divides nations.
claims.status: No count of supporting and opposing nations has been published.
